title: How NOLA and Malaco sessions were financed; Barefootin' origins
summary: Partners paid for sessions, musicians were paid more after hits; Robert Parker brought the song Barefootin', which sat on the shelf and was released on Eugene Welly's label.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well, we all, we all, we all, we all put up the money. Uh, you know, sometimes some of the musicians, uh, did it for, uh, some of the musicians did it for, uh, for not for the right, uh, right amount of money. Uh, for instance, like, it must have been, uh, it must have been, uh, a barefootin'. Like a lot of my friends came in and we did the record. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And for a small amount of fee. But you see, after the record came out and we made a little noise, and we got some money in for it, we, we took care of the musicians after that, which was our promise if it would do something, you know. Uh-huh. So we did that, but usually the guys in the, in the, in the, uh, in the organization came up with the money if it would just be for the, uh, uh, just for the session fee. And I think maybe we might have made a deal with the studio that would go 50-50 on something, something like that. You might only believe barefootin' was in, in that kind of category. Uh-huh. But, uh, Mr. Big Stuff with Gene Knight was in that, it was in that situation. Uh-huh. They paid the, they paid the musicians and supplied the studio time, and then they'll take out the studio time and what they put out for the musicians and things of that sort, and then we'll split the production money off and then we, uh, you know, we give the artists what belonged to them. But, uh, uh, with-
Do you remember something like that, the Big Stuff? Do you remember that being a special arrangement for you? Mr. Big Stuff?
I mean, not Mr. Big Stuff, Barefoot and Robert Pell. Barefoot.

Robert came in with a song. Uh, I think Euleth Gaines, I brought him in to listen to him. At that time I think he was, he was playing tennis saxophone and singing on gigs and things like that, and he came up with this song. I heard it and I said, let's try it. Uh, we went into the studio with it and it got, uh, it was on the shelf a little while.
Uh, uh, you know, and somebody remembered about it and then we put it, uh, actually it wasn't

for the normal records, it was for, uh, it was for, uh, this youngster that was on in a group with us, uh, uh, uh, Eugene, uh, Eugene, Eugene, Eugene Werley. And it was his, it was, uh, it was his label that we did it for, but we just lent him the, uh, the label to put it on. Uh, uh, you know, so there was a confusion with that. But anyway, uh.
